paragraphs: Wood modelmakers fall under O*NET 51-7031.00: they make full-size or scale precision wooden models, patterns, templates, and fixtures for products according to blueprints, drawings, or written specifications, including wood jig builders and loft workers. Excludes metal and plastic modelmakers, wood patternmakers, carpenters, wooden furniture making, and mass-production woodworking machine operation.

For a quick assessment, consider three points: can you understand drawings and specifications and confirm revisions, tolerances, and design intent; can you follow machine procedures for sawing, planing, shaping, and hand fitting and truthfully measure and record; and can you stop equipment, clarify, and escalate first when dimensions exceed tolerances, equipment is abnormal, or safety is uncertain?

Better suited to a working style involving prolonged hands-on work, sensitivity to dimensions and contours, acceptance of repeated measurement and rework, willingness to maintain patterns and records, and reliance on procedures and responsible personnel to confirm safety and quality.

These are editorial suggestions, not hiring or qualification standards. Exercises on this page use fictional drawings and dimension tables for paper exercises only, without real machine tools, cutting tools, or production systems. They do not authorize machine tool operation, safety qualifications, or design sign-off.

Wood modelmakers (O*NET-SOC 51-7031.00, Model Makers, Wood) make full-size or scale precision wooden product models according to blueprints, drawings, or written specifications, including wood jig builders and loft workers. Outputs include models, patterns, templates, and fixtures used to check product development, molds, and tooling shapes.

entries: Read blueprints, drawings, or written specifications and consult designers to determine pattern and model dimensions, shapes, and required machine setups.
Plan, lay out, and draw outlines of product units, sectional patterns, or full-size mockups.
Select wood stock, determine layouts, and mark part layouts on stock using scribers, squares, protractors, and similar tools.
Set up, operate, and adjust bandsaws, planers, and other woodworking machines to cut and shape components, parts, and patterns according to specifications.
Plane, scrape, file, and sand using hand tools to achieve specified shapes, and check model dimensions and contours using templates and measuring instruments.
Assemble wooden pieces into patterns or models using glue, nails, dowels, bolts, and similar fasteners, mark identifying information, and maintain pattern records for reference.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET Work Context survey): mainly woodworking shops and model workshops. 94% of respondents wear common protective or safety equipment daily, 84% encounter hazardous equipment daily, 73% consider exactness very important, 72% are in noisy environments daily, and 77% work 40 hours per week (U.S. respondent scope).

Required capabilities focus on drawing interpretation and layout, wood and woodworking machinery knowledge, hand fitting, measuring instrument use, and habits of procedural recordkeeping and shutdown for anomalies. The work primarily involves hands-on making, repeated measurement, and procedural review.

O*NET structured fields: interest code RCA (Realistic, Conventional, Artistic); work styles include attention to detail and dependability; principal knowledge includes production and processing, design, and building and construction; key abilities include near vision, arm-hand steadiness, and finger dexterity.

Wood modelmakers differ from adjacent occupations mainly in materials and shaping methods, precision responsibilities, and authorization boundaries. Similar titles do not make them interchangeable; verify actual target tasks and qualifications anew when transitioning.

Comparisons use O*NET occupational tasks, work activities, and work context, along with BLS/O*NET employment definitions. The following directions are real paths within the occupation or clearly adjacent occupations, not job recommendations.

Wood modelmakers produce wooden models, patterns, and layouts. The following are real adjacent occupations. Compare who defines requirements, shapes materials, measures and releases work, and bears safety and acceptance responsibility.
Focuses more on wooden patterns for casting and mold making, generally requiring material shrinkage allowances and production tolerances.
Compare this direction if you prefer combining modelmaking with production pattern design.
New hires and newcomers preparing to change careers

First master drawing interpretation, measuring instrument use, and machine safety procedures, then use tools to assist drawing and record organization without skipping mentoring or equipment authorization.
Skilled workers independently responsible for models and patterns
Use tools for process drafts and data organization, while personally remeasuring critical dimensions and tolerances and retaining traceable measurement records.
Process, quality, and tooling roles
Use tools to accelerate draft plans and checklists. Responsible personnel confirm tooling verification, first-article conclusions, and change approvals according to procedures.
Mentoring and management roles
Define tool usage boundaries and recordkeeping requirements, update training and checklists, and do not publish generated content directly as process documentation.

Insufficient evidence: a national wage distribution in mainland China corresponding one-to-one with wood modelmakers has not been obtained. Industry averages and U.S. wages cannot substitute for this occupation's median.

As proxy measures, the National Bureau of Statistics' 2025 manufacturing average annual wages were 113,594 yuan in urban non-private units and 76,055 yuan in private units. These are industry figures, not occupational or individual wages.

Average annual wages for 'production, manufacturing, and related personnel' in enterprises above designated size were 80,739 yuan (2025, including wood processing, furniture, and wood product workers, without separately identifying this occupation). This likewise cannot be rewritten as this occupation's median, percentiles, or starting wage.
For salary judgments, check the specific city, employer, job level, and published recruitment requirements, retaining region and date.

U.S. 51-7031.00 (Model Makers, Wood) had 2025 median wages of 56,550 USD/year and 27.19 USD/hour, from BLS OEWS displayed through O*NET. Applies only to this occupation, the United States nationwide, and the listed period, not starting wages or individual guarantees.

U.S. employment in this occupation was approximately 700 in 2025. The employment base is not current recruitment. Sampling error estimates have not been obtained for this page; small numbers alone do not establish statistical volatility.

U.S. employment in this occupation is projected to decline during 2025—2035 (category: -1% or lower), with approximately 100 annual openings including growth and replacement needs. This overall employment projection is not attributed to AI and is not an individual's probability of being hired.

U.S. wage and employment data corresponds only to national O*NET 51-7031.00 statistics and cannot be extrapolated to China, a specific region, or individual offers. Role comparisons also require checking industry, hours, benefits, and responsibility scope.
The median is not a starting wage, and percentiles are not newcomer, senior, or management levels. Measuring instruments, materials, and machine tool conditions change actual role conditions.

When comparing offers, retain industry tables, regional tables, and units for the same statistical period, and distinguish hourly and annual wages under BLS definitions. Do not use them to calculate individual annual or after-tax income.

entries: Prefers hands-on making, assembly, and repair of physical objects over purely verbal or abstract work.
Works according to steps and standards and accepts repeated measurement and review.
Editorial observation: whether you complete detailed work in process order and keep truthful records; do not set thresholds using conscientiousness scores.
Editorial observation: whether you are willing to learn new materials, tools, or methods within authorization and safe conditions; no openness score requirement is set.
Prefers independently completing concrete hands-on tasks with clear goals.
Can adapt to on-site pace and physical demands without relying on prolonged social interaction.
Practical, attentive to quality and order, and inclined to complete work thoroughly.
Can pause and report anomalies first rather than pushing through.
Good spatial visualization and image comprehension, translating two-dimensional drawings into three-dimensional shapes.
Can convert dimensions and compare tolerances while noticing small differences.
Can remain steady under rework and schedule pressure and follow procedures.
Can effectively discuss drawing and tolerance issues with designers and machine operators.

paragraphs: RIASEC R (Realistic) and C (Conventional) describe activity preferences only. Wood modelmakers are often drawn to hands-on making and producing measurable outcomes to standards. Fit still requires judgment through real workpieces, measurement records, and mentor feedback.
Evidence level: O*NET interests and work styles come from employed worker survey statistics for career exploration, not hiring or qualification decisions.

This checklist is an editorial synthesis and cannot replace employer machine operating procedures, dust and noise control plans, or local occupational safety regulations. Unclear matters should be confirmed by safety leads or accountable personnel.

The main pressures wood modelmakers should assess in advance are cutting risks from woodworking machinery, wood dust and noise exposure, and downstream rework caused by out-of-tolerance model dimensions and contours. Prototypes and samples, tooling and fixtures, and layout work differ in exposure and responsibility.

This module's risks draw on O*NET work context percentages, NIOSH wood dust health references, and U.S. OSHA woodworking machinery and noise standards. These are U.S. definitions and editorial syntheses, not Chinese regulations or accident rate statistics.
Affected roles: modelmaking and pattern roles using bandsaws, circular saws, planers, and sanding equipment to shape wooden parts.
Potential consequences: serious hand and eye cutting injuries, amputations or severed fingers, downtime, and lost work hours.

Editorial preparation example (not a job advertisement): official wood modelmaker tasks suggest checking drawing interpretation, bandsaw and planer operation training, dimension records, and equipment guarding. A verifiable company announcement, date, and deadline have not been obtained.

This item only organizes preparation questions for occupational tasks and does not represent universal employer requirements. Verify education, experience, and authorization against the original target job announcement and local rules.

Entry signals: education, vocational training, safety, and equipment operation authorization are different statuses. Employers generally focus on drawing interpretation, woodworking machine operation, and safety records; specifics depend on employer and local rules.

Fictional material (editorially designed, not real company data): a 'Wood model drawing A1' with a planar outline of 300 mm × 180 mm and thickness of 40 mm; two Φ20 mm through holes with centers 30 mm from the adjacent edge; mating surface tolerance ±0.5 mm; basswood material. An attached dimension table lists 6 critical dimensions and allowable deviations: length, width, thickness, hole spacing, hole diameter, and mating surface flatness.

Your task: on paper, complete layout essentials, dimension and tolerance checks, the machining sequence (stock selection→layout→sawing→planing→drilling→hand fitting→measurement), and a required measuring instrument list, and identify 3 safety and quality considerations.

Suggested deliverables: a dimension check table listing each nominal dimension, allowable deviation, and conformity decision; an operation sequence sheet; and a risk list specifying triggers, possible consequences, and responses. If a dimension lacks necessary inputs, state 'insufficient information to judge' and explain what additional information is needed.

Exercise boundaries: paper exercises only throughout; do not use real machine tools, cutting tools, wood, or production systems. This exercise does not authorize machine tool operation, safety work, or design sign-off.

Evaluate the work through review results

values: Day 1 | Choose an entry point
Compare wood modelmaking, wood patternmaking, and carpentry, choose one, and write down two questions to investigate.
Day 2 | Drawing interpretation and layout
Use 'Wood model drawing A1' above to list 6 critical dimensions, allowable deviations, and datums.
Day 3 | Operation sequence
Write the operation sequence from stock selection to measurement and label the tools and measuring instruments required at each step.
Day 4 | Dimensional decisions
Create a dimension check table and classify each dimension as conforming/out of tolerance/insufficient information, with reasons.
Day 5 | Risk list
List 3 woodworking machinery, dust, or noise risks, giving triggers, consequences, and responses for each.
Day 6 | Boundary checks
List education, training, equipment authorization, and quality release separately, identifying which require employer confirmation.
Day 7 | Review and decide
Review the week's outputs and interests to decide whether to continue, change direction, or develop fundamentals first.

method_cards.含义: Under the task-level exposure framework in ILO Working Paper 140 (2025), generative AI may partially assist drawing organization, text, and records. Core wood modelmaker tasks—drawing interpretation and layout, woodworking machine shaping, hand fitting, and precision measurement—depend on hands-on work, measurement, and on-site judgment and are not directly performed by AI.

Currently available evidence concerns task exposure, not adoption rates in wood modelmaker roles. Employer hot technologies listed by O*NET center on Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint, and Word, with CATIA and Siemens NX for CAD. ai_impact_table.responsibility_intro: The following steps describe the sequence of human controls when wood modelmakers use tools (editorial synthesis):

responsibility_steps.说明: Verify drawing revisions, specifications, materials, and design confirmation records, and define the current task scope.
Use tools only for retrieval, organization, and drafts; do not generate or modify dimensions, tolerances, or process conclusions.
Review tool-generated checklists, drafts, and calculations item by item against drawings and process documents.
Follow machine operating procedures, dust extraction, and personal protection requirements; immediately stop equipment and report anomalies.
Retain actual dimensions, rework, and pattern issuance records and submit them to accountable personnel for acceptance.

risk_rows.为什么重要: Wooden models support downstream mold and tooling checks; deviations propagate to finished products
risk_rows.控制方式: Confirm datums and tolerances before starting, remeasure with templates and instruments during work, and reinspect after reworking out-of-tolerance areas

risk_rows.为什么重要: Bandsaws, circular saws, and planers can cause cuts, amputations, and severed fingers
risk_rows.控制方式: Use guards and push tools under OSHA 1910.213, keep hands away from cutting paths, and stop equipment when anomalies arise

career_risk_cards.heading: Work pressures, risks, and boundaries for wood modelmakers

risks.mitigation: Check guards, riving knives, and push tools under OSHA 1910.213. Keep hands away from cutting paths; do not clear chips while running. Wear eye and other protection required by equipment, and avoid gloves that could become entangled.
risks.scenario: Machining on bandsaws, circular saws, or planers without guards or push tools, placing hands near cutting edges, or clearing chips and adjusting workpieces before shutdown.
risks.title: Woodworking machinery cuts and amputations

risks.affected_roles: Sawing, sanding, and chip cleanup personnel
risks.consequence: NIOSH considers wood dust a potential occupational carcinogen. Long-term exposure is associated with nasal cancer and respiratory and skin diseases.
risks.mitigation: Implement dust extraction, ventilation, and exposure monitoring. The NIOSH REL recommends TWA1 mg/m³, not an OSHA statutory limit or Chinese standard. Safety leads verify applicable regulations and select respiratory protection.
risks.scenario: Inadequate ventilation and dust extraction during prolonged sanding, sawing, or sweeping allow wood dust to accumulate in the shop.
risks.title: Wood dust exposure

risks.affected_roles: Operators near planers, bandsaws, and sanding equipment
risks.consequence: Long-term high noise exposure can damage hearing.
risks.mitigation: Control noise and conduct hearing conservation and monitoring under OSHA 1910.95; use hearing protection when needed.
risks.scenario: Prolonged work near planers, bandsaws, sanders, and similar equipment without noise control and hearing protection.
risks.title: Noise exposure

risks.affected_roles: Layout, hand fitting, and dimensional inspection personnel
risks.consequence: Out-of-tolerance models propagate errors to downstream mold and tooling checks, causing rework or scrap.
risks.mitigation: Confirm drawing revisions, datums, and tolerances before starting. Remeasure with templates and instruments during work; rework out-of-tolerance areas according to processes, then reinspect and record.
risks.scenario: Failure to verify datums and tolerances during layout or shaping, or excessive hand fitting, causes model dimensions or contours to exceed specifications.
risks.title: Dimensions and contours outside tolerances

risks.affected_roles: Personnel finishing, brushing, or spraying models
risks.consequence: Finishing solvents and droplets can irritate the skin and respiratory tract.
risks.mitigation: Work with ventilation or in spray booths according to employer procedures, wear appropriate respiratory and skin protection, and manage flammable finishes under OSHA 1910.107.
risks.scenario: Applying shellac, varnish, or wax to patterns or models with inadequate ventilation or without protection.
risks.title: Finishing chemical contact

risks.affected_roles: Personnel responsible for pattern identification, issuance, return, and version records
risks.consequence: Machining from incorrect patterns causes batch rework and makes changes difficult to trace.
risks.mitigation: Verify consistency between revisions and physical items, document issuance and returns, promptly archive old patterns, and retain pattern records for reference.
risks.scenario: Failing to update revisions after repeated pattern changes, incorrectly issuing patterns, or failing to retrieve old patterns from machine operators.
risks.title: Pattern and record version errors

description.text: Wood modelmakers make full-size or scale precision wooden models, patterns, templates, and fixtures according to drawings and specifications. This page explains task scope, U.S. BLS 2025 wages and employment, Chinese industry proxy wages, AI task boundaries, fit signals, and entry paths.

subject.name: Wood modelmakers
subject.summary: Wood modelmakers (O*NET 51-7031.00, Model Makers, Wood) make full-size or scale precision wooden product models, patterns, templates, and fixtures according to blueprints, drawings, or written specifications, including wood jig builders and loft workers. Excludes metal and plastic modelmakers, wood patternmakers, carpenters, wooden furniture making, and mass-production woodworking machine operation.
